title: Addressing patient concerns about the ‘newness’ and long-term safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists: A clinician’s guide to counseling

sections.abstract:
Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed the management of type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular health, yet some patients remain hesitant to start these therapies due to perceptions that they are “new” or unproven. This commentary equips clinicians with practical counseling strategies to reframe the “newness” narrative and address long-term safety concerns. We provide a brief history of GLP-1 from its discovery in the 1980s to nearly two decades of clinical use, underscoring that GLP-1RAs are the product of extensive research rather than experimental novelties. We compare native GLP-1 to newer agents like semaglutide and tirzepatide, highlighting structural modifications that prolong action without fundamentally altering the hormone’s mechanism. Known safety data are summarized emphasizing the predominance of mild, transient gastrointestinal side effects and the lack of evidence for feared risks like cancer along with how to discuss these points. A practical counseling checklist and sample patient-centric language are included to facilitate shared decision-making. In sum, clinicians can confidently reassure patients that GLP-1RAs are well-studied, mechanism-based therapies with millions of patient-years of experience supporting their safety and efficacy.

Keywords: Obesity, Glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor agonists, Empathy, Communication, Drug-safety
sections.introduction:
It is common for patients to express concern about starting glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA), worrying that these medications are “too new” or that their long-term effects are unknown. In reality, while GLP-1RAs may be new to an individual patient, the science behind them is extensively studied. GLP-1 is a natural gut hormone (an incretin) that was first identified in the early 1980s, building on a century of research into gut-pancreas signaling [ 1 ]. The very concept of gut hormones aiding insulin secretion, the “incretin effect” dates back to experiments in the early 20th century and was clearly demonstrated by the 1960s [ 2 ]. What patients see today as cutting-edge therapy is in fact the culmination of decades of rigorous, peer-reviewed scientific inquiry and drug development. Since the first GLP-1RA (exenatide) was approved in 2005, this class of medications has amassed extensive clinical trials and real-world usage, establishing a robust safety and efficacy record [ [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Misconceptions about GLP-1RAs being “experimental” or lacking data can thus be gently corrected by sharing this perspective: these therapies are a mature, evidence-based tools, not a shot in the dark.

Early physiological studies in 1902 by Bayliss and Starling first hinted that the gut produces factors (later called “hormones”) influencing the pancreas. The term incretin (“internal secretion”) was coined in 1932 for a gut hormone that could lower blood sugar. In the 1970s GLP-1 was identified as a second incretin hormone [ 2 , 6 ]. By 1987, GLP-1 was shown to stimulate insulin secretion in humans and rapidly became a therapeutic target. However, native GLP-1 has a short half-life (only 1-2 minutes in circulation) due to rapid enzymatic degradation by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) [ 6 ]. This hurdle led researchers to seek modified versions of GLP-1 that could resist breakdown and provide sustained action. The breakthrough came from the Gila monster snake venom yielding exendin-4, a GLP-1 mimetic that is DPP-4 resistant. Exendin-4 was developed into exenatide, the first GLP-1RA, approved in 2005 for type 2 diabetes [ 7 ]. This opened the door to a “generation” of incretin therapies ( Fig. 1 ).

Evolution of incretin therapeutics.

(A) Timeline from early gut-pancreas discoveries to modern approvals: GLP-1 identification, DPP-4 inactivation, exenatide (2005), liraglutide (2010), once-weekly agents, oral semaglutide (2019), and dual agonist tirzepatide (2022-23).

(B) Native GLP-1/GIP (t½ 1-2 min) versus long-acting analogs: liraglutide (C16 acylation; t½ ∼13 h), semaglutide (Aib 8 + C18 at Lys 26 ; t½ ∼165 h), tirzepatide (Aib 2 + C20 at Lys 20 ; t½ ∼120 h). Abbrev: Aib, α-aminoisobutyric acid; DPP-4, dipeptidyl peptidase-4.

Over the next two decades, several GLP-1RAs were introduced [ 8 ]. Fig. 1 illustrates how today’s therapies stand on a foundation of discoveries spanning over 40 years, rather than appearing out of the blue. Sharing this timeline with patients can reassure them that GLP-1RAs are not a passing fad but a well-established therapeutic class grounded in long-standing science [ 9 ].

One powerful reframing strategy is to explain that GLP-1RAs are analogs of a hormone our bodies already produce. Native GLP-1 is a 30-amino-acid peptide our gut releases when we eat, which in turn helps stimulate insulin, limit glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and promote satiety. GLP-1RAs work by the same mechanism, just with molecules engineered to last longer in the bloodstream. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prime examples of how smart molecular modifications extend the hormone’s action [ 10 ].

Native GLP-1 (and the related GIP hormone) are quickly inactivated by DPP-4, which cuts at a specific alanine near the N-terminus (position 2 of GIP, position 8 of GLP-1). Substituting alanine with a similar but DPP-4-resistant residue, α-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib), protects the molecule from degradation [ 11 , 12 ]. Additionally, attaching a fatty acid chain to the peptide enables it to bind to albumin in the blood, acting as a “shield” that slows clearance [ 13 , 14 ]. Semaglutide incorporates Aib at position 8 and a C18 fatty diacid chain at (Lys 26 ), conferring DPP-4 resistance and a ∼165 hours half-life enabling once-weekly dosing [ 13 ] Tirzepatide has Aib at the second residue and an acylated lysine (Lys 20 ) with a C18-C20 diacid resulting in a ∼120-hour half-life and weekly dosing. ( Fig. 1 , Panel B) [ 15 , 16 ] The take-home message for patients is that these drugs are 98-99 % identical to our natural hormones; the modifications simply make them work better as medicines. Thus, GLP-1RAs are not introducing some foreign chemical; they are enhancing a physiologic pathway that the body is already familiar with, which is one reason for their favorable safety profile.

Patients sometimes equate “new drug” with “unknown risk.” For many individuals, hesitation toward GLP-1RA therapy stems from broader mistrust in the healthcare system, previous negative experiences with medications, or a preference for ‘natural’ or holistic approaches. These patterns mirror qualitative research on vaccine and statin hesitancy, which shows that patients frequently want their clinician to first understand their values, beliefs, and lived experiences before accepting a therapy [ [17] , [18] , [19] ]. Using open-ended questions such as, ‘What concerns you most about starting this medication?’ or ‘What has your experience with other treatments been like?’ helps build trust and allows the patient to feel heard before data are introduced. For instance, large-scale trials of modern GLP-1RAs began over a decade ago and have enrolled over 70,000 patients collectively, with some individual trials following patients for 5-7 years. Cumulatively, semaglutide alone accounts for hundreds of thousands of patient-years of exposure across trials and real-world use [ 20 ]. In practice, millions of people worldwide have now been treated with a GLP-1RA, some for many years, providing a vast safety dataset. Regulatory agencies (FDA, EMA, etc.) have required ongoing pharmacovigilance and have not identified new serious safety signals in over 15+ years of monitoring. In fact, by 2020 the American Diabetes Association and American College of Cardiology endorsed GLP-1RAs as foundational therapy for high-risk diabetes patients given the strength of evidence [ 21 ]. A clinician might counsel a patient: “It’s understandable to be cautious with any medication, but GLP-1RAsare not an ‘untested’ novelty. These have been around since 2005 and studied in more than 70,000 people in clinical trials, plus many more in everyday practice. We actually know a great deal about their long-term effects, certainly as much as, if not more than, many older drugs that people take routinely.”

These conversations also differ depending on the patient’s clinical and financial context. Insurance coverage, out-of-pocket cost, and the patient’s treatment history strongly influence decision-making and should be acknowledged early. A clinician might say: ‘Because you already take metformin, adding a GLP-1RA can help your weight and heart health without causing low blood sugar’. Tailoring counseling language to each patient’s background and constraints respects their autonomy and increases receptiveness, even when scientific reassurance alone is insufficient.

Importantly, GLP-1RA therapies are no longer viewed solely as glucose-lowering drugs but as comprehensive cardiometabolic treatments. A growing body of evidence shows benefits extending to cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, and heart-failure outcomes. Semaglutide demonstrated significant reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events in SUSTAIN-6 and, more recently, in non-diabetic patients with established CVD in the SELECT trial [ 3 , 22 , 23 ]. Renal protection was shown in the FLOW trial, where weekly semaglutide slowed CKD progression in T2DM [ 24 , 25 ]. In parallel, GLP-1RAs and dual-/triple-incretins are emerging as disease-modifying therapies for MASH/MASLD: semaglutide improved NASH resolution in Phase II studies, while tirzepatide (SYNERGY-NASH) and retatrutide show promising fibrosis and steatosis reductions [ 26 , 27 ]. Heart-failure benefits have been demonstrated in obesity-related HFpEF through STEP-HFpEF and SUMMIT [ [28] , [29] , [30] ]. Together, these trials underscore that GLP-1RA based therapies function as multi-system CKM agents, supporting discussions with patients that their value extends far beyond diabetes control. ( Fig. 1 ) ( Fig. 2 )

Counseling pathway for “newness.”

Explain GLP-1RAs as physiologic hormone analogs; reiterate ∼20-year track record; outline benefits (glycemia, weight, CV risk); set expectations for dose-related gastrointestinal effects and slow titration; discuss rare risks (MTC/MEN2, gallbladder, pancreatitis) when relevant; review logistics (once-weekly injection or oral on empty stomach) and follow-up (∼2-week check-in, 2-3 month review); invite questions and partner on decisions.

Placing new drugs within their long developmental and clinical history reassures patients that serious long-term risks would likely have surfaced by now, while evidence instead demonstrates substantial cardiometabolic benefits alongside a well-defined safety profile.

The most common side effects with GLP-1RAs are gastrointestinal (GI); primarily nausea, which sometimes progresses to vomiting or diarrhea in some patients. Importantly, these GI symptoms are usually dose-dependent and transient: they tend to occur during dose escalation and then taper off as the body adapts. In practice, slow titration of the dose and patient coaching (e.g. eat smaller meals, avoid rich/fatty foods initially) can make this tolerable [ 21 , 31 ]. Patients often worry about feeling sick; we can set expectations by saying: “You might have some nausea at first. That's actually how we know it’s working on your appetite, but we start low and go up slowly. For most people, the nausea is mild and improves over a few weeks. Let me know if it’s more than you can manage, because we have ways to help.” Other frequently asked questions include hypoglycemia and injection reactions. GLP-1RAs by themselves do not cause low blood sugar, because their insulin release effect is glucose-dependent (unlike insulin or sulfonylureas) [ 32 ]. Only if combined with those older drugs would there be a risk of hypoglycemia. This is an important reassurance: “These medications won’t make your sugar drop too low on their own, so you’re not at risk of sudden lows.” Injection-site reactions are rare and usually minor (a small redness or bump). Many GLP-1RAs now come in user-friendly pen devices with tiny needles; even patients with needle phobia often find self-injection surprisingly easy after coaching.

Over the years, several serious risks have been postulated notably pancreatitis[ 33 ], pancreatic cancer[ 34 , 35 ], and thyroid cancer[ 35 ] but extensive research has not confirmed these fears in humans [ 36 ]. Early on, a few case reports and animal studies raised concern about pancreatitis [ 37 ]. Now, however, large analyses have found no increase in pancreatitis incidence among GLP-1RA users compared to similar diabetic patients not on these drugs [ 33 ]. One recent propensity-matched study even observed a slightly lower lifetime pancreatitis risk in GLP-1RA users (0.3 % vs 0.4 %), possibly reflecting overall better diabetes control [ 35 ]. Similarly, initial worries about pancreatic cancer have not been borne out; long-term trials and meta-analyses show no higher rates of pancreatic neoplasms in GLP-1RA groups [ 38 ].

Thyroid cancer is often brought up because of an FDA-mandated warning about medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in rodents [ 39 , 40 ]. Here it is crucial to clarify: this specific thyroid tumor was seen in rats and mice given extremely high doses of GLP-1RAs over their lifespans, but it has never been observed in humans on these medications [ [41] , [42] , [43] ]. Out of caution, GLP-1RAs are contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or the genetic syndrome MEN2 that predisposes to it [ 35 , 44 ]. For everyone else, current evidence indicates no meaningful increase in thyroid cancer risk with GLP-1RAs.

Other rare or potential risks can be discussed in context. Cholelithiasis/cholecystitis is a known but infrequent side effect, often related to rapid weight loss. Trials focused on obesity have noted an increased risk of gallbladder disease (2-3 %) with GLP-1RAs. Thus, patients should report severe or persistent right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain or nausea [ 38 , 44 ]. Evidence on GLP-1RA-associated retinopathy progression is mixed: the SUSTAIN-6 trial noted early worsening among patients with pre-existing proliferative disease, likely related to rapid glycemic improvement, while multiple meta-analyses and real-world studies have not shown increased long-term retinopathy risk. Current guidelines recommend that patients with diabetes receive an annual dilated eye exam, and a baseline exam is advisable before initiating GLP-1RA therapy in individuals with poor glycemic control or known retinopathy. Patients should be counseled to report new floaters, vision changes, or dark spots promptly [ 20 ]. Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) should also be considered in this context. Recent large cohort and pharmacovigilance studies have identified a small but statistically significant increased risk of NAION in patients prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide, particularly within the first year of use [ 45 , 46 ].
sections.conclusion: After decades of development and extensive clinical use, GLP-1RAs have proven to be safe and effective therapies for cardiometabolic disease. The perception that they are “too new” can be addressed through patient education, emphasizing that these agents amplify a physiologic hormone pathway, are supported by robust clinical and post-marketing evidence, and are generally well tolerated with manageable side effects. When patients understand that GLP-1RAs are the product of long-standing science rather than experimental shortcuts, they can make more informed decisions. By pairing clear evidence with empathetic listening, clinicians can foster shared decision-making, build trust, and help patients thoughtfully consider therapies endorsed by professional guidelines.
